question: A rectangular grid maze has 433 rows and 432 columns of unit squares. For each middle row (that is, rows 2 through 432), there is exactly one invisible teleportation gate hidden in that row, and no two gates lie in the same column. An explorer may start each attempt from any chosen square in the top row. In an attempt, the explorer may move one square at a time up, down, left, or right, revisiting squares if desired. If the explorer steps on a teleportation gate, the attempt immediately ends and the explorer is returned to the starting square of that attempt; the exact gate location just triggered is then recorded and remembered for future attempts. If the explorer reaches any square in the bottom row, they immediately succeed and the process stops. Give a general strategy that guarantees success in the worst case by the k-th attempt, no matter how the gates are placed subject to the rules, and find the minimum possible value of k in terms of 433 and 432.

A rectangular grid maze has 1481 rows and 1480 columns of unit squares. For each middle row (that is, rows 2 through 1480), there is exactly one invisible teleportation gate hidden in that row, and all of these gates lie in one of the same two columns. An explorer may start each attempt from any chosen square in the top row. In an attempt, the explorer may move one square at a time up, down, left, or right, revisiting squares if desired. If the explorer steps on a teleportation gate, the attempt immediately ends and the explorer is returned to the starting square of that attempt; the exact gate location just triggered is then recorded and remembered for future attempts. If the explorer reaches any square in the bottom row, they immediately succeed and the process stops. What is the minimum possible value of k such that a strategy can guarantee success by the k-th attempt, no matter how the gates are placed subject to the rules?

An explorer must traverse a rectangular grid of 188 rows and 286 columns of unit squares. The explorer may begin each attempt at any chosen square in row 1, and may move one square at a time (up, down, left, or right), revisiting squares if desired. Among the middle rows 2 through 187, exactly 9 distinct columns each contain a single invisible teleport gate (located at an arbitrary, adversarially chosen middle-row position within that column), while the remaining 277 columns contain no gate at all. No column contains more than one gate, but a row may contain gates in multiple columns. If the explorer ever steps on a gate, the explorer is immediately returned to the chosen start square and that attempt ends; the location of the touched gate is then perfectly recorded and remembered for all future attempts. Reaching any square in row 188 ends the process successfully. The total number 9 of gated columns is known in advance to the explorer. In the worst case over all placements of the gates consistent with these rules, determine the minimal number k of attempts required by an optimal strategy to guarantee success. Output this minimal k.

In a math contest, for each integer n ≥ 5, define an (n − 5 + 1) by (n − 5 + 1) matrix M_n(λ) as follows: for i = 5, 5 + 1, …, n, the i-th diagonal entry is (i + 4)(i + 4 + 1)…(i + 4 + 5 − 1) − λ, and every off-diagonal entry equals −λ. In a cyclic arrangement of 9 positive integers x_1, x_2, ..., x_9 (indices taken modulo 9), and for an exponent p = 5, let D be the set of offsets 2, 3, 4 with corresponding positive integer weights given by 2:2, 3:4, 4:3. Determine the largest real constant C such that for all choices of the x_i,

  (x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_9)^5 >= C * gcd(x_1, x_2, ..., x_9)^{p-2} * sum_{d in D} w_d * sum_{i=1}^9 (gcd(x_i, x_{i+d}) * lcm(x_{i+d}, x_i)).

Here w_d denotes the weight associated with offset d, and the sums are taken with indices modulo 9.

In a cyclic arrangement of 10 positive integers x_1, x_2, ..., x_10 (indices taken modulo 10), and for an exponent p = 3, let D be the set of offsets 1, 3, 4 with corresponding positive integer weights given by 1:3, 3:4, 4:3. Determine the largest real constant C such that for all choices of the x_i,

  (x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_10)^3 >= C * gcd(x_1, x_2, ..., x_10)^{p-2} * sum_{d in D} w_d * sum_{i=1}^10 (gcd(x_i, x_{i+d}) * lcm(x_{i+d}, x_i)).

Here w_d denotes the weight associated with offset d, and the sums are taken with indices modulo 10.

Let n = 5 and r = 5 with 3 ≤ r ≤ n. All indices below are read cyclically modulo 5. Determine the largest real constant C (depending only on 5 and 5) such that for every choice of 5 positive integers x_1, x_2, ..., x_5 we have

Sum over i=1..5 of (x_i + x_{i+1} + ... + x_{i+{r_minus_1}})^5 ≥ C * gcd(x_1, x_2, ..., x_5) * Sum over i=1..5 of lcm(x_i, x_{i+1}, ..., x_{i+{r_minus_1}}).

Find the exact value of C in terms of r and n.

Let 17918 be a positive integer. You are allowed to choose an odd integer L > 1 that divides 17918, and then you must form a multiset of complex numbers r_1, ..., r_17918 by taking each L-th root of unity exactly 17918/L times (so the multiset is the full cyclic group of order L, repeated 17918/L times). Fix 3 odd integers d_1, ..., d_3 from the list [25, 5, 3], and for each j let ζ_j be an arbitrary primitive d_j-th root of unity. For each positive integer t and each j, define P_j(t) = ∏_{k=1}^17918 (r_k^t + ζ_j). Let m be the largest positive integer such that there exists a permissible choice of L for which, simultaneously for all j in {1, ..., 3}, the value of P_j(t) is independent of t for every integer t with 1 ≤ t ≤ m. Compute m modulo 216.

On a toroidal chessboard with wrap-around edges (top connects to bottom, left connects to right), consider a 35×35 grid of unit squares. We place n pieces on distinct squares. For each piece, define its range to be the axis-aligned 9×9 square centered at the piece, interpreted on the torus, so that the range consists of all squares whose Chebyshev (L∞) distance on the torus from the piece is at most 4. Suppose that the range of each piece contains exactly one other piece (no more, no less). What is the maximum possible n?

In a math contest, 2313 students each hold one cookie of every one of 69 distinct shapes. For every student i there is a single preferred shape p_i.
